title: Migrations: changing a live database safely
summary: How schema changes travel from your laptop to production as files in git, and how to change a table without breaking the app that is using it.
youWillLearn: Why "works locally, breaks in production" happens with databases
What a migration file is, and how the database remembers which ones ran
Why you never edit an applied migration or click changes into production
The expand and contract pattern for renames and removals without downtime

glossary.migration: A small file, usually SQL, that changes the database schema one step, kept in git and run in order on every database.
glossary.Supabase CLI: Supabase's command-line tool. It runs a local copy of your project and manages migration files.
glossary.migration history: A table inside the database that lists which migration files have already been applied.
glossary.schema drift: When a database's real shape no longer matches what the migration files describe, usually after a manual change.
glossary.expand and contract: A way to change a schema in safe stages: add the new thing, move code and data over, then remove the old thing later.
glossary.backfill: Filling a new column for rows that already existed before it was added.
glossary.lock: A database making other queries wait while it changes a table, so they do not see a half-finished change.

steps.title: Works on my machine, breaks in production
body: Maya asks for pinned notes. Claude Code adds a pinned column to your local database, builds the feature, and it works. You push to GitHub. Vercel deploys.
Production breaks: column notes.pinned does not exist. The new code shipped, but the production database never got the column. Two copies of the database, two different shapes.

scene.caption: The code reached production. The column did not.

steps.title: Schema changes as files, in git
body: The fix: never change a database's shape by hand. Write each change as a small SQL file, a migration. Name the files by time, commit them next to the code, and run them in order on every database.
Same files, same order, same result. Local, preview and production end up with the same shape.

callout.text: A logbook of recipe changes. Instead of cooking from memory, you write each change on a dated card. Any kitchen that follows the cards in order makes the same dish.

scene.caption: Migration files live in git and flow to every database in the same order.

steps.title: One change, one file
body: The Supabase CLI creates the file for you, with a timestamp in its name so files sort in order: supabase migration new add_pinned.
Inside is plain SQL that moves the schema one step forward. Keep each file small and about one thing. Claude Code can write the SQL; the file is what makes the change repeatable.

code.code:
alter table notes
  add column pinned boolean not null default false;
code.caption: Existing rows get false, so nothing breaks for notes made before the change.

steps.title: The database remembers what ran
body: How does a database know which files it already has? It keeps a migration history: a small table listing every migration applied. Supabase keeps it in supabase_migrations.schema_migrations.
When you push, the CLI compares your folder with that list and runs only the new files, in order. Run it twice and the second run does nothing.

code.code:
# rebuild your local database from every migration
supabase db reset

# apply new migrations to the linked project
supabase db push

scene.caption: Production runs only the file it has not seen. Now the deploy works.

steps.title: Never edit history, never click-ops
body: Two habits break migrations. Editing a file that already ran: production will not run it again, so your change never arrives. Write a new migration instead.
Changing production in the dashboard: now production has a shape no file describes. That gap is schema drift, and the next fresh database, preview branch or teammate will not have your change.

callout.text: Already clicked a change into the dashboard? Bring it back into git: supabase db pull writes the remote schema into a new migration file. Then commit it.

scene.caption: A dashboard edit changes production but no file. The copies drift apart.

steps.title: Old code and new schema overlap
body: A migration and a code deploy never land at the same instant. For a while, old Notely code runs against the new schema, or new code against the old one.
So each migration must work with the code before it and the code after it. Changes that add things are safe. Changes that rename or remove break whichever version did not expect them.

scene.caption: Renaming title to heading in one go: the code still running breaks.

steps.title: Expand, then contract
body: The safe pattern is expand and contract. Expand: add the new column, keep the old. Ship code that writes both. Backfill: copy old values into the new column, then switch reads over. Contract: once no running code uses the old column, drop it in a later migration.
More steps, no downtime.

scene.caption: Four small, safe steps instead of one risky one.

notes.text: Each step is safe to deploy alone

steps.title: Renaming a column, the safe way
body: Here are the database halves of Notely's title → heading rename. Each block is its own migration file, shipped with its own deploy.
Between them, the app code changes: first it writes both columns, then it reads only heading. Only when that version is fully live does the last file run.

callout.text: When Claude Code changes the schema, check: is there a new file in supabase/migrations, not a dashboard click or an edited old file? Does it rename or drop anything that running code still uses? Did it test with supabase db reset? Ask: "Is this safe while the old code is still live?"

scene.caption: Expand, dual write and backfill are done. Contract waits for a later deploy.

steps.title: Big tables, long locks
body: Some changes make Postgres take a lock: while it scans or rewrites a table, other queries wait. On a small table, nobody notices. With millions of rows, Notely freezes.
Usual suspects: building an index (use create index concurrently), adding not null to an existing column, changing a column's type. And drop is forever, so have a backup first.

callout.text: Supabase migrations only move forward: there is no automatic undo. To reverse a change, you write a new migration. Dropped data does not come back that way, so try destructive changes on a copy first.

scene.caption: The last step is the dangerous one: it locks, and it cannot be undone.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Every schema change is a migration file in git, run in order on every database. The database's migration history makes sure each file runs once. Never edit an applied file, never click changes into production.
Old and new code overlap during a deploy, so expand first, contract later, and watch for locks on big tables.

scene.caption: Small, ordered steps that each keep the app working.

quiz.question: Right after a deploy, Notely's logs show column notes.pinned does not exist. It works locally. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Vercel cached an old build of the code.
options.why: The error comes from the database, not the code: the new code is running, and the column is missing.

options.text: The migration that adds pinned was never applied to production.
options.why: Local and production have different shapes. Apply the migration (supabase db push) and make that part of every deploy.

options.text: Postgres does not allow boolean columns named pinned.
options.why: It does. The same query works locally, which points at a difference between the two databases.

quiz.question: You spot a mistake in a migration file that already ran on production last week. What do you do?

options.text: Fix the old file and push again.
options.why: Production's migration history says that file already ran, so it will not run it again. The fix never arrives.

options.text: Fix it in the production dashboard.
options.why: That creates schema drift: production now differs from what your files describe.

options.text: Write a new migration that corrects it.
options.why: History only moves forward. A new file reaches every database, in order, the same way.

quiz.question: Claude Code proposes one migration, alter table notes rename column title to heading;, shipped in the same deploy as code that reads heading. What is the risk?

options.text: During the rollout, the old code still asks for title and fails.
options.why: Old and new code overlap. Add heading, write both, backfill, switch reads, then drop title later.

options.text: Postgres cannot rename columns that contain data.
options.why: It can, and quickly. The danger is the running code that still expects the old name.

options.text: There is no risk, because migrations run before the deploy.
options.why: Even then, the old version keeps serving requests until the new one is fully live.

takeaways: Every schema change is a migration file in git, applied in order to every database.
The database keeps a migration history, so each file runs exactly once.
Never edit an applied migration and never click changes into production. Write a new migration.
Old and new code overlap during deploys: expand first, contract in a later deploy.
On big tables, ask about locks, and take a backup before any drop.
